title: The third verb group
goal: Use the last verb group — the one ending in *-em*, whose stem likes to change — and say how often you do things, including one rule that standard English forbids but Bosnian requires: the double negative.
bekal: use verbs of the *-em* group, including *ići*, *piti*, *jesti*, and *moći*
recognize the *-ovati* group that turns into *-ujem*
say how often with *uvijek, obično, ponekad, nikad* — and use *ne* together with *nikad*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Šta radiš danas?
dialogs.intro: Late afternoon at the flat. Emir is getting ready to go out and turns to Budi, who is still at his laptop.

lines.text: Budi, šta radiš danas poslije posla?

notes: ***Idem kući* = "I'm going home".** The form *kući* isn't an ordinary locative but a frozen old form, and it means "(to) home" — your own home. Learn it whole along with its two equally frozen siblings: *idem kući* (go home), *kod kuće* (at home), *iz kuće* (from home).

**Notice the nouns changing again:** *kafa → pijemo kafu*, *poruka → pisati poruku*, *Baščaršija → na Baščaršiju*, *ljudi → gledamo ljude*. That's the object form you've now met twice, and the next unit sets it up fully. If you're starting to feel you can guess the endings yourself — that's exactly the point.

***Hoćeš li i ti?* — "do you want to (come) too?"** The verb *htjeti* (to want) is very common and irregular: *hoću, hoćeš, hoće, hoćemo, hoćete, hoće*, with the fused negative *neću, nećeš, neće…* It's also the engine of the future tense in unit 19. For now learn *hoćeš li* as one chunk meaning "do you want…?"

***Nikad nije problem* — two negatives in one sentence, and that's correct.** Bosnian requires *ne* to stay even when *nikad*, *niko*, *ništa*, or *nigdje* is already there. The full rule is below; for now just note that the sentence does not mean "it's always a problem".

**Ćevapi.** Small finger-shaped grilled minced-meat sausages, cooked over charcoal and served in *somun* bread with chopped onion and *kajmak* (a rich clotted cream). This is Bosnia's national dish, sold everywhere, and almost always counted by the piece: *deset ćevapa* is a normal portion. A portion with a drink in Sarajevo is usually cheaper than two coffees at a café with a view — hence Emir's *jeftini*.

grammars.title: The -em group — and why the dictionary form can't be trusted
body: The third and last group. The endings are as easy as the other two; what makes it tricky is that **the stem often differs from the dictionary form**. That's why this course always lists the *ja* form.
after: **The *oni* form of this group ends in *-u*.** Now all three are complete, and this is the only row that differs between the groups: *-aju* (znaju), *-e* (rade), *-u* (idu). Know those three endings and the whole Bosnian present tense is in your hands.

**The stem changes, and there's no way to guess it.** *Pisati → pišem*, *zvati → zovem*, *uzeti → uzmem*, *doći → dođem*, *reći → kažem*, *ići → idem*. Hence this course's rule: note verbs in the *ja* form, not the dictionary form. *Idem* tells you everything; *ići* tells you nothing.

**One big group that is actually very regular: *-ovati* and *-evati* → *-ujem*.** *Putovati → putujem* (to travel), *kupovati → kupujem* (to buy), *stanovati → stanujem* (to reside), *organizovati → organizujem*. This group takes in many international loanwords, so once you recognize the pattern you gain hundreds of verbs at once. Don't confuse it with *-irati*: *studirati → studiram*, *telefonirati → telefoniram*, *planirati → planiram*. Verbs in *-irati* join the *-am* group, verbs in *-ovati* the *-ujem* group.

***Moći* (can) is irregular, and its *ja* form is the same as its *oni* form: *mogu*.** *Mogu li?* means "may I?" and it's a sentence you'll use every day. After *moći* comes the dictionary form: *Mogu li pisati? Možeš li ponoviti?* Its siblings that behave the same way: *morati* (must, *moram*), *htjeti* (to want, *hoću*), *trebati* (to need, *trebam*), *smjeti* (may, *smijem*) — all set up fully in unit 11.

grammars.title: How often — and the double negative that is required
body: Frequency words go before the verb or at the start of the sentence; their position is flexible, and your ear will quickly find the natural spot.

head: Bosanski
Say it
Meaning
Example
rows: in the morning / in the evening

after: **Bosnian negation must be double.** If there is a negative word like *nikad* (never), *niko* (nobody), *ništa* (nothing), *nigdje* (nowhere), *nikako* (in no way) — the verb **still** has to take *ne*. *Nikad **ne** pijem alkohol. Niko **ne** zna. Ništa **ne** razumijem. Nigdje **ne** idem.*

**For English speakers this feels wrong** — school taught you that "I don't know nothing" is a mistake. In Bosnian it's the only correct way. What you need to train is the reflex of adding *ne*: *Nikad pijem kafu* sounds cut off and confusing, not like a charming grammar slip.

**Even when three negative words gather, they are all used:** *Niko nikad ništa ne zna* — literally "nobody never nothing doesn't know", i.e. "nobody ever knows anything". This sentence is correct, natural, and often said.

***I* means "and", but also "too, even".** *Hoćeš li i ti?* = "do you want to come too?"; *Bosanci piju kafu i u ponoć* = "even at midnight". It goes before the word being stressed. This little word works very hard in Bosnian, and recognizing it explains many sentences that felt strange at first.

blocks.text: Thirty-odd verbs that cover almost an entire ordinary day. The second column is the *ja* form — that's the one you learn, because the other five forms can be worked out from it.

Two verbs people mix up: *ići* is "go" in the sense of walking or setting off — *idem na posao* (I'm going to work). *Doći* is "come", and is almost always used for an arrival that is completed: *Dođi sutra!* (come tomorrow). And *vraćam se* means "I'm coming back" with an obligatory *se* — without *se* it means "I'm returning something".

blocks.title: The first verb worth mastering properly: ići
items: *Idem* goes with almost every preposition, and each pair has its own meaning: *idem u grad* (into town), *idem na posao* (to work), *idem kod doktora* (to the doctor's), *idem kući* (home), *idem po kafu* (to get coffee).

*Hajde!* means "come on! let's go!" and often replaces a whole invitation: *Hajde na kafu! Hajdemo!* It isn't a form of *ići* but an interjection of its own — yet in practice the two work as a pair, and *hajde* will almost certainly be the first Bosnian word you use without thinking.
